# Preface {.unnumbered}

## Building versus Engineering

The technology industry is in a headlong rush to build artificial intelligence systems. Organizations scramble to assemble models, fine-tune weights, deploy pipelines, and capture the commercial potential of machine learning. Yet a crucial distinction separates building from engineering.

To build is to assemble components until an output appears. To engineer is to understand how those components interact under the physical laws of the machine: to measure memory movement, calculate arithmetic intensity, enforce numerical invariants, and predict where execution will stall when scale changes. Much of what passes for AI development treats the underlying runtime as a black box, optimizing a loss curve while remaining blind to the memory bus.

This book is anchored on a different principle: **track the byte, not just the loss.**

A machine learning framework is systems software. When a model trains or generates a token, floating-point numbers do not compute themselves in mathematical ether. They move across physical silicon. They stream through memory buses, contend for cache lines, saturate execution units, and stall on memory bandwidth. The practitioner who understands only the loss curve is helpless when an accelerator runs out of memory, when an inference pipeline delivers 5 percent of hardware peak throughput, or when a float32 exponential overflows to infinity and a loss turns into NaN. As machine learning matures into an engineering discipline, durable value belongs to those who understand the engine room.

This book is designed as the code-level, executable companion to the broader machine learning systems curriculum at **[MLSysBook.ai](https://mlsysbook.ai)** (*Machine Learning Systems*). While MLSysBook presents the architectural concepts, hardware landscape, and distributed scaling principles across the field, TinyTorch opens the hood on the software runtime itself, walking line by executable line through how a complete framework is built.

## The Heritage: From Lions' Commentary and MIT's xv6 to Harvard's TinyTorch

We embrace a historical precedent because history proves that this pedagogical model works.

In 1976, John Lions wrote his famous commentary on the Unix Sixth Edition kernel, teaching operating systems by walking through actual lines of code. Thirty years later in 2006, Frans Kaashoek, Robert Morris, and Russ Cox at MIT revitalized that tradition by creating **xv6**: a modern re-implementation of Unix Sixth Edition. Rather than forcing students to navigate the millions of lines of C and assembly that constitute modern Linux, the MIT team presented a clean, self-contained kernel small enough to read in a semester, yet complete enough to boot on physical hardware, handle interrupts, manage page tables, and schedule processes. A generation of computer systems engineers learned how an operating system functions by reading every line of xv6.

**TinyTorch**, which we developed at Harvard University, adopts that exact philosophy for machine learning systems.

In traditional systems curricula (operating systems, compilers, or computer architecture), it is a rite of passage to build the entire system from scratch. A student in an OS class builds a miniature kernel (like Pintos, TinyOS, or xv6); a compilers student builds a toolchain from lexing to assembly; an architecture student builds a working processor. Yet, in modern machine learning education, this systems-building tradition is genuinely lacking. Students write a tremendous amount of deep learning code, scripting isolated layers or assembling pre-built modules, but they rarely build the underlying system that collectively orchestrates them from the ground up.

Compounding this educational gap, modern deep learning frameworks have become massive software infrastructure. The PyTorch repository spans millions of lines of Python dispatch wrappers, C++ ATen tensor engines, cuDNN epilogues, and CUDA kernel templates. A newcomer attempting to understand how `loss.backward()` works inside PyTorch is immediately lost in an ocean of template metaprogramming, reference counting, and vendor-specific device drivers.

TinyTorch provides the executable commentary. It is a complete, self-contained machine learning framework implemented from scratch. It contains no external deep learning dependencies. A reader can study its tensor memory layouts, write its forward activations, construct its computational graph, implement reverse-mode automatic differentiation, and trace its optimizers line by line. Nothing is hidden; no operation is relegated to a pre-compiled binary.

## The Architectural Choice: An Executable Specification

Engineering education requires honest boundaries. TinyTorch makes deliberate design choices to maximize clarity, and a reader should understand those choices from page one.

TinyTorch uses Python for framework orchestration and NumPy arrays for raw buffer storage. NumPy supplies C-contiguous memory allocations, strided addressing, and vectorized floating-point arithmetic. Python supplies the inspectable logic: how an autograd tape records operations, how parameter discovery traverses an object hierarchy, how a data loader collates batches, and how a key-value cache manages write pointers.

We deliberately do not write the core of TinyTorch in raw CUDA or C++ template code. Writing custom CUDA thread-block synchronization and PTX assembly in the foundational chapters would trap the reader in syntax and vendor compilation flags, obscuring the architectural contracts of the runtime. TinyTorch serves as an **executable architectural specification**. It allows a student to run the entire system in a standard Python debugger, place breakpoints on gradient accumulation steps, and inspect memory strides directly.

To keep the educational contracts transparent, TinyTorch maintains deliberate pedagogical firewalls, such as synchronous CPU execution and simulated quantization, which are detailed in the Introduction. To bridge this boundary, every chapter concludes with a dedicated section titled *From TinyTorch to Production*, detailing how the mechanisms modeled in TinyTorch translate to the C++ ATen runtime, NVIDIA cuDNN, CUTLASS, and Triton. Part IV (@sec-extensions) then leaves NumPy for the first time, walking TinyTorch's optional C++, Triton, and Apple GPU extensions to measure what each one gains and costs.

## Why a Generative Transformer is the Central Workload

A systems textbook requires a workload demanding enough to stress the software runtime. While toy classifiers on synthetic datasets can verify that backpropagation computes correct numerical derivatives, they cannot expose the physical memory wall. A multi-layer perceptron with a few thousand parameters fits entirely inside a CPU's L1 data cache; it experiences no memory-bandwidth starvation, requires no context caching, and reveals nothing about sequence scaling.

For this reason, **TinyGPT serves as the unifying workload of TinyTorch**. From subword tokenization and multi-headed self-attention to autoregressive generation, memory profiling, INT8 quantization, and Key-Value caching, the framework is built and optimized around a complete generative language model. By anchoring the curriculum to a modern transformer, TinyTorch ensures that every optimization technique confronts the exact computational and memory dynamics that govern modern artificial intelligence.

## Training the Next Generation of Systems Architects

Ultimately, our goal in writing this book is not merely to help readers master today's tools. Frameworks and APIs inevitably change. Libraries that dominate the industry today will eventually be superseded by new runtimes, new programming models, and new hardware architectures.

We wrote TinyTorch to train the next generation of engineers who can build the **next PyTorch**, the **next JAX**, or the next runtime that takes their place.

It is natural to ask, in an era where AI coding assistants can generate boilerplate scripts and assemble neural networks in seconds, what the value of building a system from scratch truly is. If the AI can write the code, why learn how the engine works?

The answer lies in the limits of automation. Generative AI is remarkably effective at assembling known APIs, but it struggles with novel architectural design, strict numerical invariants, and physical hardware constraints. As AI abstracts away the routine coding tasks of the past, the bottleneck in technology development shifts. The engineers of the future will not be hired to write superficial deep learning scripts: they will be hired to reason about memory physics, to debug complex latency stalls, and to architect the systems that the AI itself runs on.

The world needs more AI systems engineers. The practitioner who only knows how to prompt a language model for a PyTorch script is ultimately replaceable. The systems architect who understands how that script translates into strided memory allocations, backward-mode tape execution, and hardware-accelerated kernels is indispensable.

The fundamentals are what endure: how memory buffers are laid out and strided, how computational graphs record dependencies and execute reverse-mode differentiation, how cache lines pack quantized values, and how memory bandwidth governs execution throughput. By mastering these first principles in TinyTorch, students graduate not as passive consumers of existing software, but as the systems architects equipped to build the future of artificial intelligence.

## The Journey Ahead

This book is designed to be read with the source code open. The companion repository contains the complete, tested reference implementation. The Introduction that follows details the five-part chapter structure, the visual signposts and callout tiers, the full curriculum roadmap across our four architectural tiers, the six reading flows, and the interactive development environment.

## Author's Note: On Craft, Systems Pedagogy, and Progressive Disclosure

I learned computer systems by building them.

In computer science, that is how we master complex abstractions: we learn operating systems by writing a kernel like xv6; we learn compilers by writing an AST parser and a code generator; we learn computer architecture by designing a pipelined processor.

Yet in machine learning, that tactile, build-it-from-scratch pedagogy was missing. Most people learn deep learning as passive consumers of massive frameworks, importing a library, calling `.fit()`, and treating the underlying machinery as an opaque black box. I wanted to bring the foundational systems way of learning to a field that desperately needed it.

My goal was to give students and learners a framework that clicks together like a precision Lego set. Granted, systems engineers do not usually invent the original mathematical algorithms; the backpropagation formulation, the attention mechanism, and adaptive optimizers were created by pioneering researchers. But there is tremendous intellectual merit, craft, and discipline in understanding how those pieces actually fit together into a performant, coherent engine. I wanted learners to hold every piece in their hands: to lay out raw tensor memory, attach the autograd tape, wire up the optimizer, assemble multi-headed attention, and watch a complete GPT transformer come to life from components they engineered themselves.

Designing that progression was one of the hardest parts of this project. Progressive disclosure in a complex software stack is deceptively difficult. Every single module had to be self-contained and immediately runnable on day one, yet snap cleanly into the next module without circular dependencies, hidden global state, or hand-waving. I spent countless days and nights brainstorming, sifting through design possibilities, and writing prototypes only to tear them down when the progression did not feel natural for learners. Every abstraction boundary in this book, from keeping `Layer` minimal with explicit `forward()` and `parameters()`, to designing the four native extension points, was shaped through that iteration.

### On AI Assistance and Modern Engineering

To bring this curriculum together at the depth and rigor it required, I worked side by side with AI coding assistants. I want to be transparent about what that collaboration actually looked like:

- **The architecture, pedagogical progression, and design decisions were mine.** I decided how the pieces should fit together, what should be included in the core versus the extensions, and how to sequence the concepts so learners build real systems intuition.
- **I used AI as an untiring pair programmer and sounding board.** We used AI to help scaffold initial code blocks, generate repetitive boilerplate, write test harnesses, and translate concepts into C++ and Triton kernels.
- **We brainstormed and stress-tested relentlessly.** I used the AI to debate trade-offs, challenge over-engineered ideas (like stripping out artificial "Track A/B" groupings in favor of a flat extension catalog), and refine explanations until they were direct and clear.
- **Exhaustive verification.** We used AI to verify mathematical equations against numerical baselines in PyTorch and NumPy, construct unit test suites, run regression checks, and inspect rendered figures and tables in the compiled PDF to ensure everything met high visual and technical standards.

This is what modern engineering looks like: the human provides the domain judgment, the architectural blueprint, and the pedagogical vision; the AI provides speed, exhaustiveness, and rapid iteration.

**A thought for students and learners:**
As you work through TinyTorch, you will likely use AI tools like Cursor, Copilot, Claude, or Gemini. I encourage you to use them. But be deliberate about how you do.

If you use AI to simply generate solutions for the exercises, you skip the struggle, and the struggle is where the learning happens. You miss the visceral understanding of stride arithmetic, memory bandwidth bottlenecks, and cache locality.

Use AI the way we did: as a tireless collaborator. Ask it to explain why an unaligned vector load carries a performance penalty. Have it help you write tricky unit tests. Use it to review your code for edge cases. But make sure that you understand how every nut and bolt fits together, because in systems engineering, real mastery comes from knowing how the machine works from the ground up.

Vijay Janapa Reddi
